title: Big Data Processing with Apache Spark
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Big Data Processing with Apache Spark ##### The job that ran for nine hours and produced 40 MB A logistics analytics team in Bhiwandi — the warehousing belt just outside Mumbai — had a nightly job that summarised scan events from every hub in the country. Roughly 900 million rows a day, parquet files landing in object storage, and one question at the end: how many parcels moved between each origin-destination pair, bucketed by hour. The output was 40 MB. The job took nine hours and twenty minutes. They had thrown hardware at it twice. The cluster went from 8 workers to 24, and the runtime went from eleven hours to nine. That ratio should have been the alarm: tripling the compute bought a 17% improvement, which means the job was not compute-bound at all. When someone finally opened the Spark UI and looked at the stage timeline, the picture was obvious. One stage had 200 tasks. One hundred and ninety-eight of them finished in under 40 seconds. Two of them ran for eight hours. Two tasks. Mumbai and Delhi hubs, which between them carried about 38% of all scan events, had been hashed into two partitions, and those two partitions were being processed by two cores while 94 cores sat idle. That is the entire subject of today, compressed into one story. Spark does not make things fast because it is Spark. Spark makes things fast when your data is distributed evenly across the work, and slow — spectacularly, embarrassingly slow — when it is not. Everything below is about understanding the machine well enough to see that in advance. ##### Why distributed computing exists, and what it costs you Single-machine tools have a hard ceiling. Pandas loads everything into RAM, and its rule of thumb is that you need 5–10× the file size in memory to work comfortably. A 200 GB dataset is not a Pandas problem. Polars and DuckDB push the ceiling higher with streaming and out-of-core execution — as you saw on Day 5 — and honestly they solve a surprising fraction of "big data" problems that are actually just "medium data with bad tooling." But once your dataset genuinely exceeds what one fat machine can chew through in an acceptable window, you need many machines. Many machines means the network enters your performance model, and the network is roughly a thousand times slower than RAM. This is the central trade of distributed computing: | Operation | Rough latency | Implication | |---|---|---| | L1 cache read | ~1 ns | Free | | Main memory read | ~100 ns | Cheap | | SSD random read | ~100 µs | Noticeable | | Network round trip (same datacentre) | ~500 µs | Expensive | | Shuffling 100 GB across 20 nodes | minutes | The thing that kills your job | So the discipline of Spark performance is largely the discipline of **moving as little data across the network as possible**. ##### Spark's architecture in one picture ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Driver Program
(your PySpark script)"] --> B["SparkSession"] B --> C["Cluster Manager
(YARN / Kubernetes / Standalone)"] C --> D["Executor 1
JVM + cores + memory"] C --> E["Executor 2
JVM + cores + memory"] C --> F["Executor N
JVM + cores + memory"] D --> G["Task on Partition 1"] D --> H["Task on Partition 2"] E --> I["Task on Partition 3"] F --> J["Task on Partition N"] G --> K["Shuffle Service
(network exchange)"] I --> K J --> K K --> L["Result back to Driver
or written to storage"] ``` The vocabulary you need: - **Driver** — runs your Python code, builds the query plan, schedules work. It is a single point of failure and a single point of memory pressure. Calling `.collect()` on a 50 GB DataFrame pulls 50 GB into the driver and kills it. - **Executor** — a JVM process on a worker node with a fixed number of cores and a fixed heap. Cores determine how many tasks run in parallel on that executor. - **Partition** — a chunk of your data. One task processes one partition. If you have 200 partitions and 100 cores, Spark runs two waves of tasks. - **Job → Stage → Task** — an action triggers a job; the job is split at shuffle boundaries into stages; each stage has one task per partition. The mental model that pays off: **your parallelism is capped by your partition count, and your runtime is capped by your slowest partition.** The Bhiwandi job had 200 partitions and 96 cores, which sounds fine, until you notice that partition sizes ranged from 4 MB to 61 GB. ##### RDDs, DataFrames, and lazy evaluation Spark's original abstraction was the **RDD** (Resilient Distributed Dataset) — an immutable, partitioned collection of objects with a lineage graph describing how to recompute it if a node dies. The 2010 Zaharia et al. paper, *Spark: Cluster Computing with Working Sets*, introduced this specifically to fix the fact that MapReduce wrote to disk between every step, making iterative algorithms miserable. RDDs are still there, and you should almost never use them. The reason is the **Catalyst optimizer**. A DataFrame is a structured, schema-aware abstraction, and because Spark knows the schema and the semantics of your operations, it can rewrite your query. An RDD is a bag of opaque Python objects doing opaque Python things; Spark cannot optimise what it cannot understand. Concretely, with DataFrames you get: - **Predicate pushdown** — a `.filter()` after a Parquet read becomes a filter applied while reading, so unmatched row groups never enter memory. - **Column pruning** — selecting 3 of 80 columns means only 3 columns are read off disk. - **Constant folding, filter reordering, join reordering.** - **Tungsten codegen** — the physical plan compiles to JVM bytecode operating on off-heap binary data, skipping Python entirely for built-in functions. That last point matters enormously in PySpark. When you use built-in functions from `pyspark.sql.functions`, your Python process just builds a plan; all actual data processing happens in the JVM. When you use a Python UDF, every row is serialised out of the JVM, into a Python worker, and back. A UDF can easily be 10–50× slower than the equivalent built-in expression. **Lazy evaluation** ties it together. Transformations (`select`, `filter`, `join`, `groupBy`, `withColumn`) build a plan and do nothing. Actions (`count`, `collect`, `write`, `show`, `toPandas`) trigger execution of the whole plan at once. This is what lets Catalyst see your entire pipeline and rearrange it — but it is also why beginners are confused when a 40-line script runs instantly and then hangs for an hour on line 41. ##### The DataFrame API in practice Here is a realistic PySpark job over hub scan events, written the way you actually want to write it. ```python from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F, Window spark = ( SparkSession.builder .appName("hub-scan-aggregation") .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "400") .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true") .config("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true") .config("spark.sql.session.timeZone", "Asia/Kolkata") .getOrCreate() ) # Reading many files: Spark treats the directory as one logical table. scans = ( spark.read.parquet("s3a://logistics-lake/raw/scans/dt=2026-07-*/") .select("parcel_id", "hub_code", "scan_type", "scan_ts", "weight_g") .filter(F.col("scan_type").isin("INSCAN", "OUTSCAN")) ) hubs = spark.read.parquet("s3a://logistics-lake/ref/hubs/") # ~1,800 rows # Broadcast the small side explicitly: no shuffle for this join. enriched = scans.join(F.broadcast(hubs), on="hub_code", how="left") hourly = ( enriched .withColumn("scan_hour", F.date_trunc("hour", F.col("scan_ts"))) .groupBy("city", "zone", "scan_hour", "scan_type") .agg( F.count("*").alias("scan_count"), F.countDistinct("parcel_id").alias("unique_parcels"), F.round(F.sum("weight_g") / 1000.0, 2).alias("total_weight_kg"), ) ) ( hourly .repartition("city") # control output file layout .write .mode("overwrite") .partitionBy("city") .parquet("s3a://logistics-lake/curated/hourly_scans/") ) ``` Three things in that snippet are doing heavy lifting: the `.select()` before anything else (column pruning), the `F.broadcast()` hint (eliminating a shuffle), and adaptive query execution being switched on. ##### Spark SQL: the same engine, a different door Every DataFrame operation has a SQL equivalent, and they compile to identical physical plans. Use whichever reads better. ```python scans.createOrReplaceTempView("scans") hubs.createOrReplaceTempView("hubs") hourly_sql = spark.sql(""" SELECT h.city, h.zone, DATE_TRUNC('hour', s.scan_ts) AS scan_hour, s.scan_type, COUNT(*) AS scan_count, COUNT(DISTINCT s.parcel_id) AS unique_parcels, ROUND(SUM(s.weight_g) / 1000.0, 2) AS total_weight_kg FROM scans s LEFT JOIN /*+ BROADCAST(h) */ hubs h ON s.hub_code = h.hub_code WHERE s.scan_type IN ('INSCAN', 'OUTSCAN') GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4 """) hourly_sql.explain(mode="formatted") ``` `explain()` is the single most valuable habit in Spark work. Read it bottom-up. You are looking for four things: 1. **`Exchange hashpartitioning(...)`** — a shuffle. Count them. Each one is a full network redistribution. 2. **`BroadcastHashJoin` vs `SortMergeJoin`** — the former is cheap, the latter shuffles both sides. 3. **`PushedFilters: [...]`** in the Parquet scan — confirms predicate pushdown fired. 4. **`ReadSchema:`** — confirms column pruning; if it lists all 80 columns, your `select` is in the wrong place. ##### Partitioning, shuffles, and the actual tuning work A shuffle happens whenever a record's destination depends on its key: `groupBy`, `join` (non-broadcast), `distinct`, `orderBy`, `repartition`, window functions. Data is written to local disk on the map side, fetched over the network on the reduce side, and the number of output partitions is `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` — default 200, which is wrong for almost everyone. **Sizing rule:** aim for partitions of roughly 128–256 MB. Divide your shuffled data volume by 200 MB to get a starting partition count. 400 GB shuffled → ~2,000 partitions, not 200. **The tools you have:** - **`broadcast(small_df)`** — replicate the small side to every executor and join locally. Works when the small side fits comfortably in executor memory (default auto-threshold is 10 MB; raising `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` to 50–100 MB is common). This is the single highest-leverage optimisation in Spark, and it is exactly what the Bhiwandi team eventually needed for their hub-reference join. - **`repartition(n, col)`** — full shuffle to `n` partitions hashed on `col`. Use before a write, or to fix skew. - **`coalesce(n)`** — reduces partitions *without* a full shuffle by merging adjacent ones. Cheap, but it can starve upstream parallelism, because `coalesce(1)` before a write makes the *entire preceding stage* run with one task. - **`partitionBy(col)` on write** — physical directory layout (`city=Pune/`), enabling partition pruning for downstream readers. Choose low-cardinality columns; `partitionBy("parcel_id")` will create millions of tiny files and destroy your object store. - **`cache()` / `persist()`** — materialise a DataFrame reused across multiple actions. Only worth it if reused; caching a DataFrame used once is pure overhead. **Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)**, on by default since Spark 3.2, fixes a lot of this at runtime: it coalesces small shuffle partitions, converts sort-merge joins to broadcast joins when it discovers the side is small, and splits skewed partitions. Turn on `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled` and it would have caught Bhiwandi's Mumbai/Delhi problem automatically. **Salting** is the manual fix when AQE is not enough. You append a random suffix to the hot key to spread it, aggregate, then aggregate again: ```python SALT = 32 salted = scans.withColumn( "salted_hub", F.concat_ws("#", F.col("hub_code"), (F.rand() * SALT).cast("int")) ) partial = salted.groupBy("salted_hub").agg(F.count("*").alias("c")) final = ( partial .withColumn("hub_code", F.split(F.col("salted_hub"), "#").getItem(0)) .groupBy("hub_code") .agg(F.sum("c").alias("scan_count")) ) ``` Nine hours became eleven minutes for the Bhiwandi job: broadcast the hub table, raise shuffle partitions to 1,200, enable skew join handling. No new hardware. ##### Common mistakes - **Using `.collect()` or `.toPandas()` on a large DataFrame.** This funnels everything into the driver. Use `.limit(1000).toPandas()` for inspection, or write to storage. - **Leaving `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` at 200** for a job shuffling hundreds of gigabytes. - **Python UDFs where a built-in exists.** Check `pyspark.sql.functions` first; if you truly need custom logic, use a Pandas UDF (vectorised, Arrow-based) rather than a row-at-a-time UDF. - **`coalesce(1)` before writing a large output**, which collapses the whole upstream stage to a single task. - **`partitionBy` on a high-cardinality column**, producing the small-files problem. - **`.count()` scattered through the script for debugging** — each one triggers a full recomputation of the plan unless you cached. - **Caching everything.** Cache consumes executor memory that shuffles and joins need, and can cause spilling that is worse than recomputation. - **Ignoring the Spark UI.** The stage timeline and the task duration distribution tell you within 30 seconds whether you have skew. - **Testing only on a 10,000-row sample.** Skew and shuffle problems are invisible at small scale; you must test on a realistic slice. - **Reading CSV in production.** Parquet gives you columnar pruning, compression, and schema. CSV gives you none of it and cannot be split efficiently when gzipped. ##### Hands-on: put it on the cluster today Your practical task is to get PySpark running locally or on Databricks Community Edition, load a multi-file dataset, and do a filter, an aggregation, and a join — writing each one twice, once through the DataFrame API and once as Spark SQL. Then call `.explain()` on both and confirm the physical plans are identical. That confirmation is the point: it proves the two APIs are two front doors to one optimizer. The mini project asks for a real batch job — raw dataset in, cleaned and aggregated Parquet out, partitioned sensibly. Before you tune anything, open the Spark UI, find the shuffle-heavy stage, and record the max and median task duration. A max/median ratio above about 5 is skew. Then tune one thing and re-measure. The assignment is the discipline that makes all of this stick: take a `groupBy` + join workload, time it, then improve it by repartitioning or broadcasting the smaller table, and write down not just the speedup but *why*. "It got 8× faster because the broadcast eliminated a 340 GB exchange, visible as one fewer `Exchange` node in the plan" is an answer that shows you understand the engine. "It got faster because I added `broadcast`" is not. ##### Key takeaways - Spark's speed comes from parallelism across partitions; your job is only as fast as its slowest task, so **skew, not cluster size, is usually the bottleneck**. - **Use DataFrames and Spark SQL, not RDDs** — Catalyst can only optimise what it understands, and lazy evaluation lets it see and rewrite your whole pipeline. - **Shuffles are the expensive operation.** Count the `Exchange` nodes in `explain()`, and eliminate them with broadcast joins wherever one side is small. - **Tune deliberately:** partition sizes around 128–256 MB, `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` sized to your data, AQE and skew-join handling enabled, salting for pathological keys. - **Reach for Spark only when you need it** — a single machine with Polars or DuckDB beats a badly-tuned cluster on most datasets under a few hundred gigabytes.

RDDs vs DataFrames and lazy evaluation
Spark SQL and the Catalyst optimizer
practical_task_reference: Set up PySpark locally (or on Databricks Community Edition), load a multi-file dataset, and perform filtering, aggregation, and a join using the DataFrame API and equivalent Spark SQL.
mini_project_reference: Build a Spark batch job that ingests a large raw dataset, cleans and aggregates it, and writes partitioned Parquet output, then inspect the query plan and tune at least one shuffle-heavy step.
assignment_reference: Take a groupBy-join workload, measure its runtime, then improve it by repartitioning or broadcasting the smaller table and document the speedup and why it happened.
